records.name: Cundinamarca
records.current_summary: No department-specific legal, enforcement or incident finding was located for Cundinamarca: the country research classified it among the units whose risk sits in the national and departmental homicide counts only, without a sub-national deviation material enough to score separately (±0.02); it is therefore assessed alongside the national position.  National context from the sources: the country's monitoring bodies recorded 270 LGBTIQ+ killings in 2025 (one every 32 hours, a 63% increase on 2024's 164), with violence expanding territorially into departments where the state response is weakest; no Colombian department criminalises anything about being trans, and gender-identity recognition is administered nationally. The articles cited for this unit document the national picture (the transfeminicide in Bello, Antioquia, and armed-group 'social cleansing' in Caquetá) and none reports findings specific to Cundinamarca.

records.name: Vichada
records.current_summary: This frontier department is covered by the dedicated country dossier, which identified no department-specific legal, enforcement or incident finding beyond the national and departmental homicide counts: no deviation from the national position is material enough to score separately (±0.02), so it is assessed at the national score. Context that does apply here: Vichada sits in the country's frontier/border belt where 'orden público' regimes mean armed groups rather than departmental police effectively regulate conduct, and Caribe Afirmativo's 2025 report documents the territorial expansion of violence and insufficiency of state response, with trans women displaced from such departments because of their gender identity by the same armed actors that displace others.

sources.claim: El País in English (14 Apr 2025) on the killing of Sara Millerey (32), a trans woman, in Bello, Antioquia: beaten and thrown into a creek, died of her injuries, onlookers filmed instead of helping; the third LGBTQ+ killing in Bello in 2025; 13 trans people killed nationally in Q1 2025. National context — no Vichada-specific content.

The Guardian (30 Jul 2024): armed groups threatening a wave of 'social cleansing' against trans women in Caquetá — Tatiana Cespedes (51) given a week to leave or be killed, twice displaced; 41 trans women killed in the country in 2023, 8 killed Feb–Apr 2024; flyers circulating by WhatsApp list trans women as legitimate military targets. Documents the armed-group threat model that also applies to frontier departments including Vichada.

records.name: Santander
records.current_summary: No department-specific legal, enforcement or incident finding was located for this division. The 2025 national reporting groups it with departments where anti-LGBTIQ+ violence has expanded territorially while the state response stayed insufficient — one LGBTIQ+ person was killed every 32 hours nationally in 2025 (270 killings, a 63% increase on 2024's 164, of which 18% of the 2024 homicides were trans women). Otherwise it inherits national conditions.

sources.claim: English-language report (14 Apr 2025) on the murder of trans woman Sara Millerey, 32, in Bello, Antioquia (4 Apr 2025): beaten and thrown into a creek in daylight while bystanders filmed instead of helping; her death went viral 5 April, prompting vigils in several cities and a presidential order to investigate; the town's LGBTQ council co-director said it was the third LGBTQ killing there that year; 13 trans people were killed nationally in Q1 2025.

'We are killed for what we are' (30 Jul 2024): trans women in Caquetá threatened by armed groups after flyers announced a 'social cleansing' campaign naming 'faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes' as targets; a trans woman was given a week to leave town or be killed and fled; more than 40 trans women were killed the previous year (41 in 2023, 8 between Feb-Apr 2024); activists document sexual violence by armed groups against trans women, including former combatant recruitment.
